Published online:
    10 September 2026

Geographic focus:
    Russia (Ryazan region, ~200km southeast of Moscow); secondary relevance to Europe

Temporal focus:
    T1. Historical report [YES]
    T2. Forward-looking reporting short-term risks (next few weeks/months) [YES]
    T3. Forward-looking reporting long-term risks (next quarters/years) [NO]

Synopsis:
    Ukraine's drone strike on September 6 has forced a full operational halt at Russia's Rosneft-owned Ryazan oil refinery, the primary fuel supplier for Moscow. Two of the plant's three main crude distillation units (CDU-6 and CDU-4) are offline, representing ~180,000 bpd of processing capacity, or roughly 75% of the plant's total throughput. CDU-3 has been under maintenance since mid-May. Repairs are estimated to take up to several weeks. The refinery accounts for ~4.9% of Russian total refining capacity. This is the third drone attack on the facility in 2026, following strikes in May and July, suggesting a sustained and escalating Ukrainian campaign targeting Russian downstream energy infrastructure.

Q01. Is the content relevant to gas in terms of low supply, high demand, market crisis, physical issues? How severe is the issue?
Relevance: IMPLICIT — The article concerns oil refining, not gas directly. However, a sustained reduction in Russian refining capacity could tighten domestic fuel availability in Russia, potentially redirecting gas molecules toward domestic power/heating use and reducing Russian energy export flexibility. The recurrent nature of attacks increases forward-looking supply risk.
Severity score: Spring 10, Summer 10, Fall 15, Winter 20
